paras: The attempted lynching of Adam Jackson took place in Washington County, Tennessee, in June 1903, when a mob caught Jackson, a Black man from Charlotte, North Carolina, accused of assaulting a white woman, and put a rope around his neck. Jackson survived and was bound over to court and jailed at Jonesboro, though the local paper and the wire disagreed on how he was spared. Wire headlines such as "Mob Halts in Lynching" made the rescue the news, and a Virginia editorial cited it as proof that Southern authorities protected accused men.

According to the Johnson City Comet, Jackson worked on the railroad bridge being built across the river at Embreville and on a Tuesday morning stayed off work, saying he was sick. The woman, Mrs. Isaac Poore in the wire story and Mrs. Ike Pore in the Comet, was a farmer's wife living on Jump Hill, across the river from Embreville.

The Comet reported that Mrs. Pore, returning from washing at a neighbor's house late in the afternoon, was caught by a man she identified as Jackson and thrown down, her head striking a rock. In the Comet's account he was "frightened away by her screams without having accomplished his purpose"; the Knoxville Sentinel's special said instead that she was dragged to a thicket, assaulted, and "may die."

Neighbors and men working at Embreville organized what the Comet called a posse and went after him. Several men were brought before Mrs. Pore before she identified Jackson, who denied the charge. His captors then fastened a large rock to his neck with a rope and were ready to throw him into the river when, the Comet said, he offered to confess if they would not lynch him. The wire version, datelined Johnson City, June 11, said a mob "had strung him up when a deputy sheriff and posse arrived," and that he was taken down at the posse's appeal.

According to the Comet, Jackson confessed before the district magistrate, was bound over to court, and was taken to the Jonesboro jail "for fear he might be lynched." The wire story likewise reported a confession, a binding over to court, and confinement at Jonesboro. The Comet expected him to be allowed a trial by jury. No report of an indictment, trial, or verdict appears in the coverage, and no paper named members of the mob or reported action against them.

The Comet, published in Johnson City, gave the fullest account under the headline "Attempted Assault," with a deck calling Jackson a "Flend" [fiend] "Locked in Jail at Jonesboro, Awaiting Trial by Jury." The Knoxville Sentinel's special became a wire story that ran on June 12 in the Americus Times-Recorder, the New-York Tribune, the Savannah Morning News, and the Evening Journal. Over the next two weeks it was reprinted or condensed in weeklies from South Carolina to Mississippi.

Headlines varied: "Mob Halts in Lynching" in the Tribune, "Strung to a Tree" in Savannah, "Posse Saved Negro From Lynching" in the Evening Journal. The Hopkinsville Kentuckian chose "Criminal Assault. By Negro Brute on White Woman," and called him "Abram" Jackson. Most versions stated the assault as fact, but a variant run by the Fulton County News and the Democratic Messenger said only that Jackson "is accused of the crime."

On June 26 the Virginia Citizen reprinted a Free Lance editorial, "Where the Shoe Pinches," which set the case beside mob killings in Illinois and Indiana. It praised the Johnson City authorities, who "rescued a colored man from a mob," while stating as fact that he had "brutally assaulted a white woman." No Black-press report of the episode was found.

The Comet described a rope-and-rock threat of drowning that ended when Jackson offered to confess; the wire said he was hanged and cut down at a deputy sheriff's appeal, which the Comet does not mention. The Comet called the alleged assault a failed attempt, the wire a completed assault that might prove fatal; the Comet, reporting from Jonesboro, gave the more detailed account. The wire's "late yesterday afternoon" in a June 11 dispatch means June 10; the Comet's account can be read to place the attack on Tuesday, June 9; the editorial said "last Thursday."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Adam Jackson
bases: A mob pursued and caught Adam Jackson, accused of assaulting a white woman, and put a rope about his neck intending to kill him; he survived (A2, A3), so this is an attempted lynching.

A private mob seized Jackson over an accusation of assault on a white woman and either hanged him or threatened to drown him (A2, A3), but every report says he survived and was jailed (A2, A3, A7), so no one was killed; it was an attempted lynching.

The local Comet (A1, A2) and the separately reported Knoxville Sentinel special (A3) agree that Jackson was caught by a mob, had a rope put about his neck, confessed, was bound over and jailed at Jonesboro, though they differ on the method and on the rescue.

accounts.label: Local paper (Johnson City Comet)
accounts.gist: An attempted assault that failed; neighbors and Embreville workmen caught Jackson, tied a rock to his neck with a rope and were about to throw him in the river when he offered to confess if not lynched; the magistrate bound him over and he was jailed for his safety.

accounts.label: Wire report (Knoxville Sentinel special)
accounts.gist: A completed criminal assault, the woman perhaps dying; a mob caught Jackson and strung him up, and a deputy sheriff's posse arrived and got him taken down; he confessed and was jailed at Jonesboro.

accounts.label: Editorial (Free Lance, reprinted)
accounts.gist: Johnson City authorities rescued the man from a mob after he was hung up, which the writer contrasted with mob killings in Illinois and Indiana.

framing.detail: The local Comet called the accused a 'Flend' [fiend] in its headline but stressed that he was jailed to await 'Trial by Jury' and called the episode an 'Attempted Assault'.
Wire reprints stated the assault as fact and headlined the rescue ('Mob Halts in Lynching', 'Posse Saved Negro From Lynching', 'Strung to a Tree') or the accused ('By Negro Brute on White Woman').
The Free Lance editorial praised the Tennessee authorities' rescue while asserting the man 'brutally assaulted a white woman', using the case to defend the South against Northern critics.
